C001.title: ArmaturaSec d.o.o.
C001.text:
ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001): Cybersecurity, Zrenjanin, 67 employees, founded 2008.
ArmaturaSec d.o.o. has been building network security hardware in Zrenjanin since 2008. We started by selling simple firewall appliances to regional electricity distributors who needed to segment their control networks from corporate IT. Over fifteen years that focus narrowed: today every product we ship is designed specifically for operational technology environments — the kind of networks that run pumps, switchgear, and assembly lines, not office computers. Our customers are energy utilities, water treatment operators, and discrete manufacturers in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. They are not looking for cloud dashboards or vendor lock-in; they need a device that sits in a metal cabinet at a substation or pump station, runs for years without attention, and tells someone when something is wrong. We have 67 people in Zrenjanin. About half write firmware or do hardware bring-up; the rest handle sales, installation, and support. Our head of engineering, Radovan Čičić, joined from a SCADA integrator in 2011 and has led every product generation since. We do not resell other vendors' software. Everything that runs on our appliances — the protocol parsers, the access control engine, the alerting logic — is written and maintained by our own team.
Products: NetGuard-OT: network access control appliance for industrial Ethernet segments; NetGuard-OT Mini: DIN-rail form factor variant for smaller substations and pump stations; ProtoSense: passive protocol inspection module for Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic; ArmaturaSec Managed Support: annual firmware maintenance and remote monitoring subscription; SecAudit Report: one-time on-site assessment and written security findings report.
Tech: Embedded Linux (custom Yocto build); Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP protocol parsing; C and Rust for firmware components; iptables and nftables for packet filtering; GPRS and LTE-M cellular backhaul; Python for internal tooling and test scripts; Hardware-in-the-loop bench testing with physical PLC simulators; X.509 certificate management for device identity.
Plans: ArmaturaSec intends to release a fifth hardware variant in late 2025 with a dedicated security processor to support on-device anomaly detection without affecting packet forwarding latency. We are also evaluating whether to open a small office in Sarajevo to reduce travel time for Bosnian client support.
R&D capacity: We can dedicate one to two engineers part-time to a collaborative project, with access to our traffic archives, our hardware bench, and our existing firmware codebase under NDA.
Past collaborations: We ran a one-semester student project with a technical faculty in Novi Sad in 2021 that produced a prototype BACnet fuzzer; the code was useful but the collaboration was not continued formally.

C001-CH1.title: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.
C001-CH1.text:
We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. We have the traffic archives, we have the hardware to run inference on-device, and we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months. We need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language.

C001-CH2.title: Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.
C001-CH2.text:
Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.

Every time we release a firmware update we have to send someone to the customer site to plug in a USB drive. For a substation forty kilometres outside Novi Sad that is manageable. For a client in a mountain valley in Bosnia it means a full day of travel. We want to push updates over the cellular link the appliance already uses for remote monitoring. We have prototyped three approaches. The first used a plain HTTPS pull with a signature check; a security review inside the team found the key storage on the current hardware was not good enough and an attacker with physical access could extract the signing key. The second used a dual-partition scheme with rollback; it worked fine on a stable connection but when the GPRS link dropped mid-transfer the bootloader left the device in a state we could not recover remotely, which is unacceptable at an unmanned site. The third prototype added a download manager with resume support but the code size pushed us over the flash budget on our older hardware variant. We need a design that tolerates interrupted transfers, does not require hardware we cannot retrofit, and does not introduce a new remote code execution path. We have a draft threat model document we can share.

C001-CH3.title: Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.
C001-CH3.text:
Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.

Four clients — three in Serbia and one in Bosnia — have asked us to attach a euro figure to each finding in our SecAudit reports. They want to be able to tell their board: this vulnerability could cost us this much. We understand why they ask. They need to justify remediation budgets. The problem is we have never done this and we are not sure our current data supports it. We have records of what the vulnerabilities were, we know roughly what downtime costs for a water utility or an electricity distributor, and we can find published incident cost studies from Western Europe. What we do not have is a repeatable calculation method that holds up when a procurement officer asks how we arrived at the number. We have looked at two published frameworks and found them either too abstract or built for IT environments where data breach costs dominate. Our clients care about production downtime, regulatory fines under Serbian energy law, and emergency response costs. We need a methodology we can apply consistently across different client types, document in a way that survives scrutiny, and run with our existing audit team without hiring a financial analyst.

C001-CH4.title: Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.
C001-CH4.text:
Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.

We release firmware roughly once a month across four hardware variants: the original NetGuard-OT board, the Mini, and two older boards we still maintain for clients under long-term support contracts. Before each release our QA team runs a regression suite that they have been building by hand since 2015. The suite now has around 1,400 test cases. Writing new cases for a feature, updating old ones when hardware behaviour changes, and running everything on four boards takes about two and a half weeks of engineering time per cycle. That is the 35% figure. We have also shipped three bugs in the past year that the regression suite should have caught but did not because the relevant test cases were out of date. We have tried generating tests from our internal protocol specifications but the tooling we built for that was brittle and the team abandoned it. We want to get to a point where adding a feature automatically produces a skeleton of tests that a junior engineer can complete in an hour rather than a day. We are open to any approach that fits inside our existing Python-based test runner and does not require us to replace the hardware bench we already have.

C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.id: C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection
C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.title: Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection
C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.text: For about eighteen months we tried to build a detection component that could identify unusual Modbus traffic by training on labelled datasets published by research groups. We had four datasets we thought were credible. We spent a significant chunk of time getting them into a format our pipeline could use, training classifiers, and then testing them against real traffic from our own lab bench and from anonymised captures our clients had agreed to share with us. The results were not good. False positive rates that looked acceptable on the test set turned into something much worse when we applied the model to a real site. A water treatment plant runs its Modbus polling on a rhythm that is specific to that plant — the scan rate, the register addresses, the devices on the bus, everything. A model trained on traffic from a research testbed in another country does not know that rhythm. It cannot know it. We also noticed that the labelled datasets we were using represented attack scenarios that were either very obvious (flooding the bus with write commands) or very specific to hardware we do not see in the Balkans. Neither is particularly useful. What we think actually works for our environment is learning what normal looks like on a specific site and flagging deviations from that. No labels, no pre-trained model from somewhere else. This is not a new idea. The challenge is doing it in a way that runs on our hardware, produces alerts that a plant operator can understand without a data science background, and does not require us to collect six months of clean traffic before it is useful. We have not solved this yet. We have a set of traffic archives from our client base and one engineer who has been working on this part-time. If you have relevant experience or want to talk about it, we are interested.

C001/job/2024-02-05/Firmware Engineer —.title: Firmware Engineer — Network Protocols (Zrenjanin)
C001/job/2024-02-05/Firmware Engineer —.text:
ArmaturaSec is looking for a firmware engineer to join our core development team in Zrenjanin. We have a monthly release cycle across four hardware variants and we need someone who can contribute to protocol parsing, system integration, and the tooling that keeps the whole process running. What the work looks like day to day: you will work on the firmware that runs on our NetGuard-OT appliances — mostly C with an increasing share of Rust for new components. You will work closely with the person responsible for our Yocto build system and with the QA team that tests each release on physical hardware. We deal with Modbus TCP, BACnet/IP, and a few less common industrial protocols. You do not need to know all of them when you start. You do need to be comfortable reading protocol specifications and writing parsers from them. The hardware side: our appliances are based on ARM Cortex-A SoCs. We have a bench in the office with physical boards, PLC simulators, and packet generators. You will spend time at that bench. What we are looking for:
— At least three years writing firmware or embedded systems software in C
— Comfort with Linux networking internals (netfilter, raw sockets, that level)
— Experience debugging with JTAG or serial console, not just printf
— Some exposure to Rust is useful but not required What we are not looking for: someone who wants to work on cloud infrastructure or web services. This is hardware-close work. We offer a permanent contract, a salary in line with the Zrenjanin market for this experience level, and flexible hours within reason. The office is in the industrial zone on the north side of the city. Remote work is possible one or two days a week once you are settled in. Send a CV and a short note about something you have built to [email removed].

C001/job/2024-03-12/QA and Test Automati.title: QA and Test Automation Engineer (Zrenjanin)
C001/job/2024-03-12/QA and Test Automati.text:
Our QA team maintains a regression suite of around 1,400 test cases that runs against every firmware release on four hardware boards. The suite is written in Python and runs against physical hardware on a test bench. It works, but it is slow to extend and we are spending too much engineering time on it. We are looking for someone who wants to take ownership of that suite and make it better. That means maintaining what is already there, finding ways to generate or scaffold new test cases faster, and reducing the manual effort involved in keeping tests up to date when firmware behaviour changes. This is not a role where you will be asked to deploy a commercial test management platform and declare victory. We have specific constraints: the test runner is Python, the hardware is physical and will stay physical, and the timeline for releases is not going to change. What we need is someone who will sit with the existing code, understand why it is the way it is, and improve it incrementally. Some things that would be useful background:
— Experience maintaining a large test suite in Python
— Familiarity with hardware-in-the-loop testing or any kind of test automation that involves real devices rather than simulators
— An opinion about why test suites grow brittle over time and what to do about it Experience with industrial protocols is not required. You will learn what you need to know about Modbus and BACnet on the job. The role is full-time in Zrenjanin. One or two days remote per week is possible. We expect some collaboration with our firmware engineers and some with the field support team who often find bugs first. Questions and applications to [email removed]. We review applications on a rolling basis.

C001/website/2024-01-15/What We Do — Arm.title: What We Do — ArmaturaSec d.o.o.
C001/website/2024-01-15/What We Do — Arm.text: ArmaturaSec builds network security appliances for operational technology environments. If you run a water treatment plant, an electricity distribution substation, or a manufacturing line and you need to control who can talk to your PLCs and whether that traffic looks legitimate, that is what our products are designed for. We are not a general-purpose cybersecurity company. We do not sell endpoint agents, email filters, or cloud security platforms. Every product we have shipped since 2008 has been a hardware device that sits inside an industrial network and inspects or controls traffic at the protocol level. Our NetGuard-OT appliance handles network access control: it enforces rules about which devices can communicate, blocks unauthorised connections, and logs everything in a format that your existing SCADA historian can ingest. The Mini variant fits on a standard DIN rail for installations where cabinet space is limited. ProtoSense is our protocol inspection module. It understands Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP at the message level, not just the packet level, so it can tell you that a device sent a write command to a coil it has never written to before — not just that traffic occurred. Our SecAudit service is a one-time on-site engagement. Two of our engineers spend two days on your site, map the network as it actually exists, identify the gaps between that and how it is supposed to be configured, and produce a written report with prioritised findings. We work with clients in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Most of our installations are in the energy and water sectors. A growing share are in food and beverage manufacturing. If you want to talk about a specific installation or you have a question about whether our products fit your environment, contact our sales team in Zrenjanin.

C005.title: Kardiolink a.d.
C005.text:
Kardiolink a.d. (C005): Medtech and digital health, Novi Sad, 112 employees, founded 2004.
Kardiolink a.d. has been designing and manufacturing cardiac monitoring devices in Novi Sad since 2004. We started as a small team of electrical engineers and cardiologists who believed that continuous ECG monitoring should not require a hospital stay. Twenty years later, we employ 112 people across hardware design, firmware, clinical affairs, and software, and our patches are used by cardiology clinics and remote patient monitoring programmes in fourteen EU countries. Our core product is the KL-Patch line: single-use, adhesive ECG patches that patients wear for up to 72 hours while going about their normal lives. Clinicians receive processed reports through our cloud-based KardioPortal platform. We handle everything from electrode chemistry and PCB layout to the signal processing algorithms and the regulatory documentation that lets our devices reach patients legally. What keeps us grounded is that we manufacture in-house at our Novi Sad facility. We control tolerances, can trace every component, and can respond to field feedback without waiting on a contract manufacturer. Our clinical team works directly with cardiologists at partner clinics to make sure what we ship is actually useful at the bedside, not just impressive on a datasheet. We are a mid-size company and intend to stay close to the product.
Products: KL-Patch 72: 72-hour single-use adhesive ECG monitoring patch; KL-Patch 14: 14-day extended-wear cardiac event recorder; KardioPortal: cloud platform for ECG data management and clinical reporting; KL-Reader: clinic-side docking station and data upload terminal; Custom OEM patch manufacturing for third-party remote monitoring programmes.
Tech: ADS1293 and ADS1298 analog front-end ICs for ECG acquisition; nRF52840 SoC for Bluetooth Low Energy communication and firmware; FreeRTOS on ARM Cortex-M4 for embedded firmware; Lossless ECG compression using modified SZ algorithm; AWS S3 and Glacier tiered storage for signal archives; IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle toolchain (Jira, Confluence, Polarion); Altium Designer for PCB layout and design verification; Python and MATLAB for signal processing algorithm prototyping.
Plans: Kardiolink plans to launch the KL-Patch 14 in the German and Dutch markets following CE MDR certification and to expand KardioPortal with a structured reporting module aimed at high-volume cardiology outpatient departments. Over the following two years we intend to grow the device fleet to 6,000 active patches per month and bring cloud infrastructure costs back in line with 2022 levels.
R&D capacity: We have twelve people working across hardware, firmware, and algorithm development, with a shared lab equipped for electronics prototyping, signal acquisition testing, and device-level EMC pre-compliance testing.
Past collaborations: Between 2019 and 2021 Kardiolink worked with the engineering faculty in Subotica on a student project to evaluate alternative electrode materials, which informed the adhesive layer redesign in the KL-Patch 72 revision three.

C005-CH1.title: Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.
C005-CH1.text:
Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. We have already tuned BLE advertising intervals and moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and we switched to a lower-power MCU variant last year. We are now within a few milliamps of what we think we can achieve through firmware changes alone. We need someone who understands the full power budget — radio duty cycling, ADC configuration, memory access patterns — and can find where the remaining headroom is. The constraint is hard: sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. We have instrumented reference hardware in our lab with a Keysight N6705C power analyzer and can provide full current profiles to anyone working on this.

C005-CH2.title: We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.
C005-CH2.text:
We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.

Each KL-Patch 72 device generates roughly 900 MB of raw 16-bit ECG samples over its wear period at 250 Hz across three channels. We are deploying around 2,200 devices per month and growing. Our current pipeline applies a lossless compression step before upload, and the best we consistently achieve is 3:1, which still leaves us pushing about 2 TB to cloud storage each month. At €7,400 per month that is already a significant operating cost, and if we hit our projected 4,000 devices per month by Q2 next year the bill more than doubles. We looked at moving to lossy compression but our regulatory submission is built around lossless, so changing that requires a new clinical validation study and amendments to the technical file — not something we can do quickly. We also explored cold storage tiering and that saves maybe 15%, not enough. What we actually need is a better lossless algorithm that understands the structure of ECG signals: the quasi-periodic nature, the baseline wander, the noise characteristics of a wearable electrode. We have a labelled dataset of about 140,000 30-minute segments we can share under NDA for algorithm development and benchmarking.

C005-CH3.title: Our CE MDR technical file was submitted eight months ago and the notified body has come back with 23 queries about our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304; we do not have in-house regulatory affairs staff experienced with the new MDR annexes and hiring one is taking longer than expected.
C005-CH3.text:
Our CE MDR technical file was submitted eight months ago and the notified body has come back with 23 queries about our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304; we do not have in-house regulatory affairs staff experienced with the new MDR annexes and hiring one is taking longer than expected.

We submitted our CE marking technical file under MDR in July last year. The notified body, Zertivo GmbH, came back four months later with 23 written queries. About 18 of the 23 concern our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304, specifically the traceability between our risk management records under ISO 14971 and the software safety classification rationale, and the completeness of our verification and validation activity records. We built our QMS years ago under the old MDD and have been adapting it incrementally, but the MDR annexes — particularly Annex I and the software-specific parts of Annex II — are much more demanding. We have two quality engineers on staff who are competent at our manufacturing QMS but have not worked through an MDR submission before at this level of detail. We posted a regulatory affairs manager role three months ago and have not found the right candidate. We need practical help drafting responses to these 23 queries and updating the underlying documentation. The notified body has given us a six-month window to respond before the file lapses. Missing that window means restarting the submission, which would cost us at minimum one full year and delay entry into two new national markets.

C005/blog/2023-11-14/What We Learned at.id: C005/blog/2023-11-14/What We Learned at Meditech Forum Vienna 2023
C005/blog/2023-11-14/What We Learned at.title: What We Learned at Meditech Forum Vienna 2023
C005/blog/2023-11-14/What We Learned at.text: Three of us from Kardiolink — Nenad Lazić from hardware, Milena Kovačević from clinical affairs, and myself from product — spent two days at Meditech Forum Vienna in October. It is a mid-size conference, more working meeting than showcase, and that suits us. Here is what we took away. The storage problem is not ours alone. In three separate conversations with engineers from other patch and implantable monitoring companies, the same topic came up without us raising it: the cost of storing raw biosignal data in the cloud is becoming a real operating expense, and the standard compression approaches people adopted four or five years ago are not keeping up with the volume growth. One engineer from a company making implantable loop recorders mentioned they had started archiving processed feature vectors rather than raw signals for older recordings, which raises obvious questions about what you lose and whether regulators will eventually have a view on it. We are watching that conversation carefully. MDR timelines are compressing everyone. Several smaller device companies said they had paused new product development to focus entirely on getting existing products through MDR certification. That is a reasonable short-term choice but it means the market for new devices is going to feel thin for another year or two while the backlog clears. For us, getting the KL-Patch 14 certified promptly is commercially important for exactly that reason: the window before competitors catch up is not infinite. Cardiologists want simpler reports, not more data. Milena spent most of her time in the clinical sessions. The consistent message from cardiologists in primary and secondary care was that the value of remote monitoring is being diluted by platforms that surface too much raw information and not enough clear clinical signal. That is useful feedback for where we take KardioPortal's reporting module next year. We will be back at Meditech Forum next year. If you are attending and want to talk patches, platform, or OEM manufacturing, reach out before the event.

C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.id: C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems
C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.title: Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems
C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.text:
Kardiolink is looking for an embedded firmware engineer to join our device team in Novi Sad. The role sits within a group of five firmware engineers responsible for the software running on our KL-Patch devices. What you will work on: Our patches run FreeRTOS on an ARM Cortex-M4, with a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 handling both application logic and BLE communication. The work involves writing and optimising firmware for real-time ECG acquisition at 250 Hz, managing BLE duty cycling to reduce active current draw, and maintaining the IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle artefacts our notified body requires. We have a specific near-term problem we need help with: our 72-hour patch consumes more current during BLE activity than we want, and we need an engineer who can dig into the power budget at the level of radio scheduler configuration, ADC sampling modes, DMA transfers, and sleep state transitions. We have a Keysight N6705C power analyser set up in the lab and a suite of instrumented reference boards ready to go. What we are looking for:
- Three or more years writing firmware in C for Cortex-M microcontrollers
- Direct experience with Nordic nRF52 series and the nRF5 SDK or nRF Connect SDK
- Demonstrated work on BLE power optimisation: advertising intervals, connection parameters, PHY selection
- Familiarity with FreeRTOS task scheduling and its interaction with low-power modes
- Ability to write and maintain IEC 62304 software lifecycle documentation is a significant plus
- Experience with biosignal acquisition hardware is welcome but not required The position is full-time, on-site in Novi Sad, with some flexibility for remote days after an initial settling-in period. Salary is negotiable based on experience. Send your CV and a short note about a power optimisation problem you have solved to [email removed].

C009.title: LinguaBot d.o.o.
C009.text:
LinguaBot d.o.o. (C009): Conversational AI, NTP Novi Sad, 22 employees, founded 2020.
LinguaBot d.o.o. was started in 2020 by three engineers who had spent years watching Serbian-language customer support run on copy-pasted email templates and overloaded call centres. We build conversational AI products specifically for Serbian-speaking users, which sounds narrow until you realise almost no one else bothers to do it properly. Our first client was a regional bank in Vojvodina; today we serve four banks and two telecoms providers across Serbia, handling roughly 140,000 chat sessions per month. Our team of 22 people sits inside the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad — mostly engineers, with a small product team and two computational linguists who focus exclusively on Serbian morphology and dialect variation. What makes us different is that we do not drop a generic multilingual model on top of a client's FAQ and call it done. We maintain our own annotated Serbian-language datasets, we run our own fine-tuning pipelines, and we treat morphological variation and script mixing as first-class engineering problems rather than edge cases. Clients stay with us because the bot actually understands what their customers type, not just the textbook version of it.
Products: LinguaBot Assist — multi-turn customer support chatbot for web and mobile; LinguaBot Search — knowledge-base retrieval with morphology-aware indexing; LinguaBot Studio — no-code flow builder for client content teams; LinguaBot Analytics — conversation quality dashboard with intent drift alerts; Managed integration service for core-banking and CRM connectors.
Tech: Python; Elasticsearch; LLM APIs (external, fine-tuned adapters); FastAPI; PostgreSQL; Docker / Kubernetes; spaCy with custom Serbian morphological components; WebSocket-based real-time chat infrastructure.
Plans: Voice channel in 2027.
R&D capacity: Four ML engineers.
Past collaborations: Internships for FTN students.

C009-CH1.title: Our search misses answers because Serbian words change form (e.g. 'kartica', 'karticu', 'karticom') and users mix Latin and Cyrillic.
C009-CH1.text:
Our search misses answers because Serbian words change form (e.g. 'kartica', 'karticu', 'karticom') and users mix Latin and Cyrillic.

Serbian is a heavily inflected language, so a single noun like 'kartica' (card) appears as 'karticu', 'karticom', 'kartice', 'karticama' depending on case, and verbs shift even more. On top of that, our users freely switch between Latin and Cyrillic script mid-sentence — sometimes mid-word in typos. Our current Elasticsearch setup uses a basic stemmer that was built for Croatian and misses a significant share of Serbian-specific forms. We have measured this: in a sample of 12,000 real support queries from one bank client, about 18% returned no useful result, and our analysis traced more than half of those misses directly to morphological mismatch or script confusion. We have tried adding synonym lists and a simple script-normalisation step, but maintaining those lists manually does not scale as clients add new product terminology every quarter. We have a labelled query-response dataset of around 85,000 pairs across all clients, and our two in-house linguists can annotate or validate proposed solutions. We need an approach that handles lemmatisation or indexing in a way that is accurate for Serbian, tolerates script mixing automatically, and can be updated when new vocabulary arrives without a full re-index. A good outcome is getting that 18% miss rate below 5% and keeping it there with a manageable maintenance process. Budget for tooling or data work is modest — around 8,000 EUR — and we want something testable within six months.

C009-CH2.title: Clients want the bot on the phone too; speech recognition for Serbian is poor on call audio.
C009-CH2.text:
Clients want the bot on the phone too; speech recognition for Serbian is poor on call audio.

Three of our bank clients have asked us to put the bot on their inbound phone lines by the end of 2027, and one telecom client has written it into a contract renewal that goes up for review in early 2027. The problem is that Serbian automatic speech recognition is genuinely poor on real call-centre audio: background noise, regional accents, fast speech, and the particular compression artifacts that come from telephony codecs all combine to produce word-error rates that make the transcript nearly unusable for intent detection. We tested two widely used commercial ASR APIs last year — neither is designed for Serbian — and word-error rates on a 300-call sample were above 38%, which is too high for reliable downstream understanding. We have a corpus of about 1,200 anonymised and consented call recordings from one client, covering a range of speaker ages and regional accents, but that is not enough to fine-tune a robust model from scratch on our own. We have four ML engineers, but none of them has deep experience in speech model training specifically. We are not expecting a production-ready ASR system from a collaboration — what we need is a clear view of what data we would need to collect, what modelling approach is realistic given our constraints, and ideally a small proof-of-concept that shows whether fine-tuning an existing multilingual model on our 1,200 recordings moves the needle enough to justify the larger data-collection effort. Timeline is firm because of the contract.

C009/blog/2024-05-22/Why our search stil.id: C009/blog/2024-05-22/Why our search still fails some of the time, and what we are doing about it
C009/blog/2024-05-22/Why our search stil.title: Why our search still fails some of the time, and what we are doing about it
C009/blog/2024-05-22/Why our search stil.text: We track every session where our bot returns no useful result. Last quarter, across all deployments, that number was higher than we want it to be — around 17% of sessions ended without the customer getting an answer. We have looked at the logs carefully. Script mixing accounts for some of it: a user types 'kredit' in Latin and our index has the document filed under Cyrillic 'кредит', or the other way around. That is solvable with normalisation and we have a partial fix in place, but it is not complete. The bigger problem is morphology. Serbian is an inflected language. The noun 'kartica' (payment card) appears in our users' queries as 'karticu', 'kartice', 'karticom', 'karticama', and a handful of other forms depending on what the user is trying to say. Our stemmer treats these as different words. Sometimes they land on the right document anyway because the document also uses multiple forms. Often they do not. We have tried expanding synonym lists manually, but our clients add new product names and terms every quarter and we cannot keep up. We have also tried a retrieval approach that uses sentence embeddings rather than keyword matching, and it helps with paraphrase variation but does not reliably fix morphological mismatch — the embedding models available for Serbian are trained on limited data and have their own gaps. What we have that could help: 85,000 labelled query-response pairs, two linguists who know Serbian morphology well, and a clear evaluation setup so we can measure whether a proposed change actually improves things before we deploy it. We do not have a clean solution yet. We are talking to people who work on computational morphology for South Slavic languages and running our own experiments on lemmatisation pipelines. If you have worked on this problem — the practical engineering side, not just the theory — we are interested in talking. You can reach us at [email removed].

C009/job/2024-04-10/NLP / Search Enginee.title: NLP / Search Engineer — LinguaBot d.o.o.
C009/job/2024-04-10/NLP / Search Enginee.text:
We are looking for an engineer who wants to work on Serbian-language search and retrieval. The core problem: our Elasticsearch-based search works, but it does not work well enough. Serbian morphology means the same concept appears in many surface forms, and our users mix Latin and Cyrillic script. We have measured a meaningful miss rate on real queries and we want to fix it properly. What you would work on:
- Improving our indexing pipeline to handle morphological variation in Serbian, whether through better lemmatisation, morphological analysis, or a different retrieval approach entirely
- Building or integrating script normalisation that handles Latin/Cyrillic mixing reliably
- Evaluating changes against our labelled query dataset (around 85,000 query-response pairs)
- Working with our two in-house linguists, who can annotate and validate What we are looking for:
- Solid experience with Elasticsearch or a comparable search system
- Python — we use it for everything in the pipeline
- Some practical experience with morphologically complex languages, or genuine interest in learning
- Comfort working with annotated datasets and running your own evaluations Nice to have:
- Experience with spaCy or similar NLP libraries
- Familiarity with Serbian, Croatian, or another South Slavic language What we do not need: a researcher who wants to publish. We need someone who wants to ship something that works and can tell when it does not. This is a full-time position at our office in NTP Novi Sad. We offer a competitive salary by local market standards, flexible hours, and a small team where your work is visible. Send a CV and a short note about what you have worked on to [email removed].

C009/job/2024-06-03/Speech / ML Engineer.id: C009/job/2024-06-03/Speech / ML Engineer (Voice Project) — LinguaBot d.o.o.
C009/job/2024-06-03/Speech / ML Engineer.title: Speech / ML Engineer (Voice Project) — LinguaBot d.o.o.
C009/job/2024-06-03/Speech / ML Engineer.text:
We have a contract commitment to deliver a voice channel product by early 2027. We need an engineer who knows how speech recognition systems work and can help us figure out what is realistic for Serbian on telephony audio. Background: we tested two commercial ASR APIs on a sample of real Serbian call recordings and got word-error rates above 38%. That is not usable. We have about 1,200 consented call recordings from a client, which is a start but not a lot. We need someone who can look at this situation clearly and tell us what is possible, then help build it. What the role involves:
- Assessing what fine-tuning an existing multilingual speech model on our data would actually achieve
- Identifying what additional data we would need to collect and how
- Building a proof-of-concept pipeline: audio in, transcript out, good enough to run intent detection on
- Working with our ML engineers on integrating ASR output into the existing chat understanding stack What we are looking for:
- Experience training or fine-tuning speech recognition models — we do not need someone who has only used APIs
- Python
- Honest about what is hard and what is not
- Able to work toward a fixed deadline without pretending uncertainty does not exist Familiarity with Serbian is not required but would help. This is a full-time position in Novi Sad. The project has a real deadline and a real budget. If you have done this kind of work before and want a concrete problem to solve, write to [email removed] with 'Voice' in the subject line.

C012.title: Sentinel Byte preduzetnik
C012.text:
Sentinel Byte preduzetnik (C012): Cybersecurity, Subotica, 6 employees, founded 2021.
Sentinel Byte was started in 2021 by Dragan Kovačević and his son Nikola Kovačević in Subotica. Dragan spent over twenty years maintaining IT infrastructure for a regional logistics company before deciding to put that experience toward helping smaller organisations understand their actual security exposure. Nikola came in from a computer science background with hands-on experience in network scanning and web application testing. Together they built a six-person team that covers penetration testing, security audits, and basic security consulting for clients across northern Vojvodina. Our clients are mostly small and medium businesses — accountancy firms, medical clinics, small manufacturers — and a handful of local municipalities who have formal obligations under Serbian information security regulations but limited in-house expertise to meet them. We do not sell fear. We run structured tests, document what we find in plain language, and sit with the client until they understand what each finding means for their daily operations. What separates us from larger firms is geography and availability. We are based in Subotica, we know the local regulatory environment, and our clients can call Dragan or Nikola directly. Six people means no account managers and no hand-offs. Every engagement is run by someone who also wrote the test plan.
Products: External and internal network penetration testing; Web application security audit; Security posture assessment for small municipalities; Post-audit remediation walkthrough session; Phishing simulation and basic staff awareness workshop.
Tech: Nmap and Nessus for network scanning; Burp Suite for web application testing; Metasploit Framework for exploitation validation; Kali Linux as primary testing environment; Custom Bash and Python scripts for reconnaissance automation; Markdown-based reporting templates converted to PDF; Git for version-controlled test documentation.
Plans: Over the next twelve months we want to add one junior tester and move at least part of our reconnaissance workflow onto an automated platform so we can offer continuous monitoring as a service. We are also looking to formalise our training offering into a product we can price and repeat.
R&D capacity: Nikola Kovačević can dedicate roughly two days per week to a collaborative development project, primarily on tooling and automation topics.
Past collaborations: Informal technical consultation with a Subotica-based IT services firm, Netlogika d.o.o., during a joint client engagement in 2023; no formal research or university collaborations to date.

C012-CH1.title: We run manual penetration tests that take our team about two weeks per engagement; clients are asking for continuous testing and retest after patches, but at our size we simply can't bill enough hours to make that sustainable — we need a way to automate at least the reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration phases.
C012-CH1.text:
We run manual penetration tests that take our team about two weeks per engagement; clients are asking for continuous testing and retest after patches, but at our size we simply can't bill enough hours to make that sustainable — we need a way to automate at least the reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration phases.

A standard engagement for us runs about two weeks: a few days of reconnaissance and enumeration, then active testing, then a reporting phase. That rhythm works when a client wants a point-in-time audit once a year. The problem is that several clients — especially the two municipalities and a regional medical supply company — have started asking us to retest after they apply patches, and one of them mentioned they want something closer to monthly checks on their external attack surface. We simply do not have the hours to bill that at our current rates and stay profitable. We have tried writing Bash scripts to partially automate the initial scanning phase, and that saves maybe two hours per engagement, but it is fragile and hard to maintain. We need a more reliable pipeline that can run scheduled reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration, flag changes since the last scan, and hand results to our testers in a structured format. If we could cut the first phase from four days to one, we could take on retest work without adding headcount. Budget for tooling or a development collaboration is limited — roughly 3,000 to 5,000 euros — but we are open to a research arrangement where the output is a working prototype.

C012-CH2.title: Two municipalities hired us and then couldn't act on our findings because their IT staff didn't understand the remediation steps; we'd like a structured training programme we could sell alongside the audit, but writing curriculum and measuring knowledge retention is not something we know how to do.
C012-CH2.text:
Two municipalities hired us and then couldn't act on our findings because their IT staff didn't understand the remediation steps; we'd like a structured training programme we could sell alongside the audit, but writing curriculum and measuring knowledge retention is not something we know how to do.

After finishing audits for two municipal clients, Opština Kanjiza and a second municipality we are not naming publicly, we delivered detailed reports and then watched nothing get fixed for three months. When we followed up, the honest answer from their IT coordinators was that the remediation steps read like a foreign language to them. We ran two informal afternoon sessions explaining the findings in plain terms, and that actually helped — one municipality patched four out of seven critical issues within a month afterward. So we know training works, but right now we deliver it informally and for free because we have no product to charge for. We would like to build a short structured programme — probably four to six modules — that we can sell as an add-on to any audit. The challenge is we do not know how to design curriculum properly, how to test whether people retained anything, or how to keep the material updated as the threat landscape changes. We have the technical content in our heads. We need help turning it into something repeatable and measurable. A good outcome would be a pilot programme we could test with one municipality client by the end of this year.

C012-CH3.title: We've been trying for five months to register as a certified auditor under the Serbian Information Security Law so we can bid on public procurement contracts, but the paperwork at the Ministry keeps bouncing back for minor formal reasons and we don't know how to fix it.
C012-CH3.text:
We've been trying for five months to register as a certified auditor under the Serbian Information Security Law so we can bid on public procurement contracts, but the paperwork at the Ministry keeps bouncing back for minor formal reasons and we don't know how to fix it.

Serbian law on information security requires that organisations in certain sectors use certified auditors for their mandatory audits. That certification would open public procurement to us, which currently we cannot bid on at all. We applied to the Ministry five months ago and have had the application returned three times, each time with a short note citing a formal deficiency. The first return was about the formatting of an attached document. The second was about a reference number on a supporting form. The third cited an unclear clause about professional experience documentation. We have tried reading the relevant rulebook ourselves and consulting a general business lawyer in Subotica who was honest enough to say she does not know this specific regulatory area well. We are not looking for legal advice in the strict sense — we just need someone who has successfully navigated this specific process and can look at our application package and tell us concretely what is wrong. A good outcome is a submitted application that does not come back. We would like to resolve this within the next three months because there is a municipal procurement round opening in the autumn that we want to be eligible for.

C012/blog/2024-04-02/Why we wrote our ow.id: C012/blog/2024-04-02/Why we wrote our own reconnaissance scripts and why we are about to stop
C012/blog/2024-04-02/Why we wrote our ow.title: Why we wrote our own reconnaissance scripts and why we are about to stop
C012/blog/2024-04-02/Why we wrote our ow.text: For the past two years, every penetration test we run has started the same way: Nikola sits down with a target scope, runs a set of Bash scripts that wrap Nmap and a few other tools, and spends most of a working day cleaning the output into something our testers can actually use. The scripts work. They are also held together with more string than we would like to admit. We wrote them because we needed something faster than running tools manually and we could not justify the licensing cost of a commercial continuous scanning platform for a firm our size. The scripts do their job: they take a list of IP ranges or domains, run a structured scan sequence, and produce a text file organised by host with open ports, detected services, and Nessus findings cross-referenced. Nikola knows every line. Nobody else on the team fully does. The problem has two parts. First, clients are starting to ask for something closer to continuous monitoring — not an annual test but a monthly or quarterly scan that shows what changed since last time. Our scripts were built for a single run, not for comparison across time. We have tried adding a diff step and it mostly works, but edge cases cause enough noise that someone still has to review everything manually before we trust the output. Second, the scripts break when tool versions change. Nessus in particular has changed its output format twice since we wrote the parser. Each time, Nikola spends two days fixing things instead of running tests. We are not complaining. We knew what we were building. But we have reached the point where maintaining this ourselves is not the best use of our time, and we are actively looking for a better approach — whether that is a different toolchain, a collaboration that could help us build something more robust, or a combination of the two. If you work on this kind of problem and want to compare notes, reach out.

C012/job/2024-03-05/Part-time Technical.title: Part-time Technical Writer / Training Developer (contract)
C012/job/2024-03-05/Part-time Technical.text:
This is a contract role, not a full-time position. We are looking for a person who can help us turn technical security content into structured training material for non-technical audiences. **Background**
We conduct security audits for small businesses and municipalities. After delivering reports, we often find that clients struggle to act on the findings because the concepts are unfamiliar to their staff. We have run informal explanation sessions that work well, but we want to formalise this into a repeatable training product we can offer alongside audits. **What we need help with**
- Structuring four to six training modules covering topics such as patch management, password policy, phishing recognition, and basic network hygiene
- Writing participant materials that a person with no security background can follow
- Designing short assessments — quizzes or practical exercises — so we can confirm knowledge retention after each module
- Advising on how to keep the material updated without rebuilding everything from scratch each year **What you need to bring**
Experience designing training or educational content for working adults. You do not need a security background — we will supply the technical content. You do need to be comfortable interviewing subject-matter experts (us), structuring information logically, and writing plainly. **Format and compensation**
This is a project-based contract. We estimate the initial build at roughly forty hours of work. Compensation is negotiable. If the product works well with pilot clients, we would like to discuss a longer-term arrangement for updates and new modules. Contact Dragan Kovačević at [email removed].

C012/news/2023-11-08/Sentinel Byte compl.id: C012/news/2023-11-08/Sentinel Byte completes first municipal engagement in Kanjiža
C012/news/2023-11-08/Sentinel Byte compl.title: Sentinel Byte completes first municipal engagement in Kanjiža
C012/news/2023-11-08/Sentinel Byte compl.text: We finished our first full security assessment for a municipal client in northern Vojvodina in October and we want to write briefly about what that experience taught us, without sharing any findings that belong to the client. The engagement covered the municipality's internal network, their public-facing web presence, and the workstations used by administrative staff. The scope was agreed over two meetings with their IT coordinator, a practical person who was candid about the limits of what he could realistically fix given the municipality's maintenance budget and procurement constraints. We found what we generally find in organisations of this type: a mix of well-maintained systems and systems that have not been touched in years because nobody flagged them as a priority. The report we delivered listed seventeen findings across four severity levels. The top three were straightforward to fix with no budget — configuration changes and a patching task that had been deferred. The more interesting outcome came a month later. We followed up with the IT coordinator and learned that only four of the seventeen findings had been addressed. Not because the municipality disagreed with our recommendations, but because the remediation steps, written in our standard technical format, were not actionable for someone who manages IT part-time alongside other administrative duties. We went back for a half-day session, went through each finding verbally, and helped prioritise. Within three weeks, eleven of the seventeen findings were resolved. This is not a story about a client failing. It is a story about the gap between a technically correct report and a useful one. We are working on closing that gap as a formal part of what we offer. If you have had a similar experience with audit reports that did not lead anywhere, we are interested in talking.

C018.title: DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o.
C018.text:
DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o. (C018): Automotive and mobility software, Novi Sad, 27 employees, founded 2004.
DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o. was founded in 2004 by Miroslav Vučić, a mechanical and electronics engineer who spent fifteen years at a German Tier-1 supplier, and his son Andrej Vučić, who joined after finishing his electrical engineering degree in Novi Sad. The two of them started with three workstations in a rented room and a single contract to port BSW modules for a mid-size European passenger car program. Twenty years later we are a team of twenty-seven engineers, all based in Novi Sad, and we have delivered software integration work on more than forty OEM projects. We focus entirely on AUTOSAR-based embedded software: configuration, integration, and V-cycle testing for powertrain, body and chassis ECUs. We do not build hardware, we do not sell IP, and we do not resell tools. Customers come to us because we do one thing and we do it carefully. Our engineers work directly inside the customer's development environment, using their toolchains and following their process rules. Our main customers are Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers delivering ECUs to European OEMs. We have worked with companies such as Hartfeld Automotive Systems (Germany), Rennova Electronics (Czech Republic) and Balkon Drive Solutions (Slovakia). Most contracts run between six and twenty-four months. What keeps customers coming back is straightforward: we document everything, we flag problems early, and we do not hide schedule risk.
Products: AUTOSAR Classic BSW configuration and software component integration; V-cycle test planning, execution and coverage reporting for ECU software; CAN, LIN and Ethernet communication stack integration and validation; ECU flashing, diagnostic tooling and UDS/OBD-II protocol support; AUTOSAR toolchain migration and legacy codebase porting.
Tech: AUTOSAR Classic (R4.x) and Vector DaVinci Configurator; CAPL scripting and CANoe/CANalyzer for network simulation and testing; TRACE32 and JTAG-based ECU debugging; Jenkins-based CI pipelines for build and static analysis; LDRA Testbed and gcov for branch and MC/DC coverage measurement; UDS (ISO 14229) and OBD-II (ISO 15031) diagnostic protocol implementation; Python scripting for test automation and report generation; MISRA-C:2012 compliance checking with PC-lint Plus.
Plans: DriveLogic Vojvodina plans to add a second delivery team by end of 2026 so we can run two large OEM projects in parallel without resource conflicts. We are also evaluating whether to extend our service scope to cover AUTOSAR Adaptive on high-performance compute platforms, which several of our existing customers are beginning to ask about.
R&D capacity: We can dedicate one senior engineer part-time (roughly 40% of their working week) to a collaborative development or research activity, provided it is directly tied to tools or methods we will use in active projects.
Past collaborations: We worked informally with a controls research group at a technical institute in Subotica around 2019 on a model-based calibration study, but the output was not published and there was no formal agreement.

C018-CH1.title: We manually generate around 3,200 AUTOSAR software component configuration files per project and it takes two engineers three weeks; one of our competitors apparently automated this and turned around the same job in four days — at current rates we are losing bids on price.
C018-CH1.text:
We manually generate around 3,200 AUTOSAR software component configuration files per project and it takes two engineers three weeks; one of our competitors apparently automated this and turned around the same job in four days — at current rates we are losing bids on price.

Every new project hands us a System Extract from the customer and we then have to produce AUTOSAR SWC configuration files — port definitions, inter-runnable variables, timing constraints, the lot — by hand inside DaVinci Configurator. On the last two projects we counted roughly 3,200 files each time. Two senior engineers spend three weeks doing nothing else. We have tried building Excel-based templates to speed up the repetitive parts, and that helped a little, but the real problem is that the mapping logic between the System Extract and the final ARXML is still done by a person reading a document and typing. We heard from a contact at a Romanian company that they built something — probably a script or a generator layer on top of the tool API — that brings the same volume of work down to four days. We do not know the details. We have the DaVinci API documentation and we have two engineers who write Python, but nobody has had time to build the tooling properly. We are losing price-sensitive bids. A good outcome is a generation process that gets us from a clean System Extract to a reviewable first-draft configuration set in under one working day, with engineers only doing review and exception handling.

C018-CH2.title: Our test coverage reports show 87% branch coverage but we keep finding integration bugs in the CAN communication stack after delivery; we suspect the problem is at the boundary between components from different suppliers but we have no systematic way to find those interaction faults before shipping.
C018-CH2.text:
Our test coverage reports show 87% branch coverage but we keep finding integration bugs in the CAN communication stack after delivery; we suspect the problem is at the boundary between components from different suppliers but we have no systematic way to find those interaction faults before shipping.

Our LDRA reports consistently show 87–89% branch coverage before we ship, which satisfies the contract threshold. But in the last four delivered projects, three of them came back with CAN communication faults found during customer integration testing. In each case the fault was at a boundary: one SWC from us, one SWC or COM configuration from a different supplier, both conforming to spec individually but producing unexpected behaviour when connected. We have tried adding integration test cases that exercise the COM layer explicitly, but we write those tests based on our own reading of the interface specification, so we tend to test what we already think is correct. We do not have a systematic way to generate tests that specifically target the assumptions each component makes about what the other will send. We have full access to the ARXML descriptions of all components in the project, the COM configuration, and the CANoe environment. What we need is a method — or tooling — that reads those descriptions and generates test scenarios aimed specifically at the interface contracts between components from different sources. Budget is not fixed but we would not start something that cost more than €40,000 in the first phase.

C018-CH3.title: Three of our five engineers who do ECU flashing and diagnostic tooling learned on the job and have no formal training in UDS or OBD-II protocol internals; last year two of them left for a bigger company in Novi Sad within 18 months of joining and we had to restart their replacements from scratch — the training cost alone was over €25,000 each time.
C018-CH3.text:
Three of our five engineers who do ECU flashing and diagnostic tooling learned on the job and have no formal training in UDS or OBD-II protocol internals; last year two of them left for a bigger company in Novi Sad within 18 months of joining and we had to restart their replacements from scratch — the training cost alone was over €25,000 each time.

Five engineers handle ECU flashing and diagnostic work. Three of them learned by sitting next to a more experienced colleague and reading our internal cheat sheets. They can operate the tools but when something unusual comes up — a NRC they have not seen, a timing issue during a diagnostic session, a service routine behaving differently on a different ECU variant — they escalate to Andrej or to our one engineer who has formal protocol training, and that creates a bottleneck. The deeper problem is retention. In the last two years we lost two of those five engineers to a larger company in Novi Sad that offered higher salaries. Each time we had to hire a replacement and start from scratch. We calculated the internal training cost each time at just over €25,000, and that does not count the three to four months of reduced output while the new person gets up to speed. We have tried writing better internal documentation and we ran one informal workshop, but it was not systematic. We want something that a new hire can work through at their own pace and that tests their understanding before they touch a real vehicle. A structured, self-contained training path for UDS and OBD-II internals, ideally with practical exercises on simulated ECUs, would let us onboard faster and reduce how much senior engineer time gets burned on repeated explanations.

C018/blog/2024-04-18/What we learned fro.id: C018/blog/2024-04-18/What we learned from four integration faults in twelve months
C018/blog/2024-04-18/What we learned fro.title: What we learned from four integration faults in twelve months
C018/blog/2024-04-18/What we learned fro.text: Over the last twelve months we had four CAN communication faults reported by customers during their own integration testing — after we had already delivered. Each one cost us time to diagnose and fix, and two of them required a re-delivery with a new test report. That is not acceptable at the rate we want to work, so we spent some time in February pulling the four cases apart to see what they had in common. In every case the fault was at a component boundary. One SWC sending a signal with an assumption about update timing. Another SWC on the receiving side, from a different supplier, with a different assumption. Both components passed their own module tests. Both matched the interface specification as written. The fault only appeared when they were connected and running on the same OS schedule. Our coverage reports showed 87–89% branch coverage in all four projects. That number did not predict the faults at all. Branch coverage tells you whether your test cases reached the code. It does not tell you whether your test cases asked the right questions about what happens when two components disagree about the timing, range or sequence of a shared signal. We have known for a while that interface testing is weaker than module testing in our process. What this review made concrete is that we do not have a systematic method for generating test cases that specifically target the contract between two components — and that writing those cases by hand, based on our own reading of the spec, tends to reproduce our assumptions rather than challenge them. We do not have a solution yet. We are looking at what information is already available in the ARXML and COM configuration that could drive a more targeted test generation step. If you have worked on this problem or have a view on it, we are genuinely interested in talking — reach us at [email removed]. Miroslav Vučić wrote the first version of this post. Andrej edited it.

C018/website/2024-01-15/Services — Drive.title: Services — DriveLogic Vojvodina
C018/website/2024-01-15/Services — Drive.text:
What we do DriveLogic Vojvodina provides software integration and testing services for automotive ECU projects built on the AUTOSAR Classic platform. All work is carried out by our in-house team in Novi Sad. We do not subcontract. AUTOSAR Configuration and Integration
We take your System Extract and deliver a complete, compiled, and reviewed BSW and SWC configuration ready for the next phase of your V-cycle. We work in DaVinci Configurator and follow your project's coding and naming conventions from day one. Typical project size ranges from 800 to 3,500 ARXML files. V-Cycle Testing
We write and execute software-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop, and on-target test suites. We use LDRA Testbed for structural coverage measurement and CANoe for network-level validation. We deliver a coverage report and a defect log at each milestone. Our standard contract threshold is 85% MC/DC on safety-relevant modules, though we work to whatever target your customer specifies. CAN / LIN / Ethernet Communication Stack Support
We configure and validate COM, PDU Router, and transport layer modules, and we write CAPL-based test scripts for frame-level and signal-level validation on the bench. Diagnostic Tooling and ECU Flashing
We write and maintain UDS service handlers, configure the Diagnostic Communication Manager, and produce the ODX/CDD files your after-sales tooling needs. We also set up and document flashing procedures for production and end-of-line environments. Toolchain Migration
If you are moving from an older AUTOSAR release or from one toolchain vendor to another, we have done this migration several times and can provide a structured plan with known risk points documented up front. Where we work
Most of our contracts are with Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers. We embed into your process rather than running a parallel one. If you use a specific configuration tool version, a specific CI system, or a specific code review workflow, we follow it. Get in touch
Send a project brief to [email removed] or call us at the number below. We normally respond within one business day.

R0057.title: Lazar Šarić
R0057.text:
Lazar Šarić (R0057): Assistant Professor, Department of Mathematics and Informatics, Faculty of Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Signal Processing; Data Compression and Coding; Biomedical Informatics; Machine Learning.
Keywords: signal compression; physiological time series; quasi-periodic redundancy; entropy coding; ECG compression; wavelet transform; learned compression; lossless coding; sparse representation; beat segmentation.
Bio: Lazar Šarić completed his undergraduate and master's studies in mathematics and computer science at the Faculty of Sciences, University of Novi Sad, graduating in 2010 and 2012 respectively. He received his PhD from the same faculty in 2017, with a dissertation on adaptive transform coding of quasi-periodic biomedical signals. Following a postdoctoral stay at the Technical University of Graz (2017–2019), he returned to Novi Sad as an assistant professor. His group focuses on lossless and near-lossless compression of physiological time series—ECG, PPG, and EEG—using discrete cosine and wavelet transforms, sparse coding, and, more recently, learned entropy models based on small recurrent networks. Teaching covers data structures, information theory, and signal processing. The group uses a shared Linux cluster in the Faculty computing lab and collaborates with the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina for annotated signal datasets.
Open to: joint projects on embedded or real-time biomedical signal compression; contract research on codec design and evaluation for medical device manufacturers; industrial PhD supervision for candidates with a signal processing or machine learning background; consulting on compression standard compliance (SCP-ECG, HL7 FHIR waveforms); student internships for final-year or master's students from partner faculties.
Industry experience: Šarić carried out a short consultancy engagement in 2022 with Mediconn d.o.o., a Novi Sad-based medical device startup, advising on the selection and parameter tuning of an ECG compression module for their Holter recorder firmware.
Notes: Šarić has expressed interest in collaborating with companies at NTP Novi Sad working on wearable health devices or remote patient monitoring platforms, particularly where real-time or near-real-time compression on constrained hardware is a bottleneck. He is not seeking purely data-science or AI engagements unrelated to signal compression.

R0064.title: Zsuzsanna Molnár
R0064.text:
Zsuzsanna Molnár (R0064): Full Professor, Department of Business Informatics, Faculty of Economics in Subotica, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Information Systems; Business Administration and Management; Organisational Behaviour; Technology Management.
Keywords: ERP implementation failure; change readiness; resistance to change; post-go-live knowledge transfer; SME digitalisation; organisational change management; enterprise resource planning; IT adoption; knowledge retention; process mining.
Bio: Zsuzsanna Molnár received her BSc and MSc in Business Informatics from the Faculty of Economics in Subotica, University of Novi Sad, graduating in 1998 and 2001 respectively, and completed her PhD at the Budapest University of Economic Sciences in 2007, focusing on ERP adoption barriers in transitional economies. She joined the Faculty of Economics in Subotica as an assistant professor in 2008 and was promoted to full professor in 2019. Her research group investigates why ERP implementations fail in small and medium-sized enterprises, with particular emphasis on change readiness assessment, employee resistance patterns, and the erosion of system knowledge after go-live. She teaches Enterprise Systems Management and Organisational Change at undergraduate and postgraduate levels, and her group routinely uses SAP training environments, process-mining tools such as Celonis Academic Edition, and survey platforms for longitudinal data collection.
Open to: joint projects with technology partners operating ERP platforms in the SME segment; contract research on ERP implementation diagnostics and post-go-live auditing; consulting engagements on change readiness assessment and knowledge retention planning; industrial PhD supervision for candidates employed at ERP vendors or implementation consultancies; student internships at NTP Novi Sad companies engaged in ERP adoption or digital transformation.
Industry experience: Between 2003 and 2007 Molnár worked part-time as an implementation consultant for a regional ERP reseller serving Vojvodina manufacturing firms, which directly informed her research focus on go-live failures and post-implementation knowledge loss. She has since maintained an advisory relationship with two regional implementation consultancies on a non-exclusive basis.
Notes: Molnár is the current head of the Department of Business Informatics and carries a high administrative load; she is best approached for collaborations with a clear practical output such as a tool, dataset, or training programme rather than purely theoretical work. She has expressed interest in collaborating with NTP companies that generate ERP transaction log data that could be used in process mining studies under appropriate data sharing agreements.

R0071.title: Olivera Rakić
R0071.text:
Olivera Rakić (R0071): Assistant Professor, Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Machine Learning and Data Mining; Signal and Time-Series Analysis; Industrial Fault Detection and Diagnostics; Pattern Recognition.
Keywords: anomaly detection; imbalanced learning; semi-supervised classification; concept drift; time-series; high-dimensional data; oversampling; real-time inference; fault detection; ensemble methods.
Bio: Olivera Rakić received her B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in Computer Engineering from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, in 2010 and 2012 respectively, and her Ph.D. from the same institution in 2018, with a dissertation on semi-supervised detection of rare fault events in industrial sensor streams. She held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Zagreb from 2018 to 2020 before returning to Novi Sad as an Assistant Professor. Her group focuses on anomaly detection and classification in high-dimensional, heavily imbalanced time-series data, including methods for handling concept drift and label scarcity. She teaches courses on machine learning and data mining at undergraduate and master level. The group makes regular use of the Faculty's data analytics cluster and has access to a small edge-computing testbed for real-time inference experiments.
Open to: joint projects with companies on anomaly detection in industrial sensor data; contract research on imbalanced classification and concept drift adaptation; industrial PhD supervision (co-supervision with company mentor); student internships for master students working on real company datasets; consulting on evaluation methodology and validation protocol design for ML-based monitoring systems.
Industry experience: During her postdoctoral period at the University of Zagreb, Rakić participated in a six-month consulting engagement with a regional utility company to audit the evaluation practices of their existing predictive maintenance classifier, resulting in a revised validation protocol. She has no other formal industry employment.
Notes: Rakić is currently co-supervising two PhD students under DRIFTGUARD and has limited capacity for new long-term commitments before mid-2025. She is particularly interested in partners who can provide access to real labelled or partially labelled sensor datasets, which are the main bottleneck for her research. She prefers collaborations where the company has an internal technical contact who can validate domain assumptions.

R0083.title: Dušan Milošević
R0083.text:
Dušan Milošević (R0083): Research Associate, Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: speech technology.
Keywords: automatic speech recognition; speech synthesis; Serbian; call centres; noise robustness.
Bio: Dušan Milošević is a Research Associate at the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, working within the Department of Computing and Control Engineering. His research focuses on speech technology for the Serbian language, spanning automatic speech recognition, text-to-speech synthesis, and robust acoustic modelling under real-world noise conditions. Between 2018 and 2021 he contributed directly to industry by building the speech processing pipeline for a commercial call-centre product, an experience that shapes his continuing interest in deployable, telephone-quality speech systems. He is currently open to industrial PhD supervision and joint research projects with companies seeking to integrate spoken-language interfaces into their services.
Open to: industrial PhD supervision; joint projects.
Industry experience: Built the speech pipeline of a call-centre product (2018–2021).

R0131.title: Željko Uzelac
R0131.text:
Željko Uzelac (R0131): Senior Research Associate, Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications, Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Обрада говорног сигнала; Аутоматско препознавање говора; Рачунарска лингвистика; Машинско учење.
Keywords: препознавање говора деце; акустичко моделовање; морфолошки богати језици; адаптација говорника; прозодија јувенилних говорника; језички модел; регуларизација; српски говор; дубоке неуронске мреже; обука на малим корпусима.
Bio: Жељко Узелац дипломирао је на Факултету техничких наука Универзитета у Новом Саду 2005. године, где је одбранио и докторску дисертацију 2013. године на тему акустичког моделовања говора деце у условима шума. Запослен је на Департману за енергетику, електронику и телекомуникације у звању вишег научног сарадника од 2019. године.
